solution.concept_anchor: Mansehra Shahbazgarhi Kharosthi-Prakrit — both in Pakistan
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because Kandahar is the most famous non-Brahmi inscription site in the northwest, and students may associate it with Kharosthi-Prakrit when it is actually Greek-Aramaic.
elimination_logic: The blank requires sites where Prakrit Major Rock Edicts were written in Kharosthi rather than Brahmi.
Eliminate (b): Taxila's Ashokan inscription is in Aramaic, not Kharosthi-Prakrit.
Eliminate (c): Kandahar's inscription is in Greek and Aramaic, not Kharosthi-Prakrit.
Eliminate (d): Laghman inscription is in Aramaic only — not Kharosthi-Prakrit.
Confirm (a): Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are the two canonical Kharosthi-Prakrit Major Rock Edict sites, both in present-day Pakistan.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The northwest has multiple inscription sites (Kandahar, Taxila, Laghman, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) and students who broadly associate the entire northwest with 'non-Brahmi inscriptions' may not precisely recall which sites use Kharosthi-Prakrit vs. which use Aramaic vs. Greek-Aramaic. Kandahar's fame as the most prominent frontier site makes it the most tempting wrong answer for Kharosthi-Prakrit — when in fact Kharosthi-Prakrit is confined to Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra.
solution.final_explanation:
Among all Ashokan inscription sites, only two produced Major Rock Edicts in Prakrit written in Kharosthi script.

• Option (a) — Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra: Correct. Both sites are in present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, in the ancient Gandhara region. Their inscriptions reproduce the Major Rock Edicts in Prakrit encoded in Kharosthi — the northwest's right-to-left, Aramaic-derived script.
• Option (b) — Taxila and Laghman: Incorrect. Both sites have Aramaic inscriptions — not Kharosthi-Prakrit. Taxila's Achaemenid administrative heritage made Aramaic appropriate; Laghman similarly used standalone Aramaic.
• Option (c) — Kandahar and Taxila: Incorrect. Kandahar is the Greek-Aramaic bilingual site; Taxila is Aramaic-only. Neither uses Kharosthi.
• Option (d) — Laghman and Kandahar: Incorrect. Both are in Afghanistan and use Aramaic (and Greek in Kandahar's case) — not Kharosthi-Prakrit.

Value Addition:
• Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are approximately 100 km apart — both in the Peshawar basin area of ancient Gandhara.
• Kharosthi's right-to-left direction matches the Aramaic script from which it derived.
• The two Kharosthi-Prakrit sites and the three Aramaic/Greek sites define the linguistic boundary of Brahmi's reach in the northwest.

solution.concept_anchor: Maski 1915 discovery — Minor Rock Edict naming Ashoka explicitly
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) pairs the Maski edict with 1905, which sounds plausible — students who know the discovery was in the early 20th century may confuse 1905 with 1915.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the correct date: Maski Minor Rock Edict was discovered in 1915 — not 1905, not 1925, not 1935.
Eliminate (a): 1905 is a temporal-swap — close to 1915 but incorrect.
Eliminate (b): 1925 is ten years after the actual discovery — incorrect.
Eliminate (d): 1935 is twenty years after the actual discovery — incorrect.
Confirm (c): Maski edict discovered in 1915 — this is the correct pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The year 1915 is specific enough that students who vaguely remember 'early 20th century' will not reliably distinguish it from 1905 or 1925. The temporal-swap between 1905 and 1915 is particularly effective because both fall in the same historical context (pre-independence colonial archaeology) and neither year has an obvious distinguishing memory hook. Only precise recall of the 1915 date secures the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maski Minor Rock Edict is the most important single edict for the identification of Ashoka as the 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' of the inscriptions.

• Option (a) — Maski edict discovered in 1905: Incorrect. The year is ten years early — a temporal-swap trap. 1905 has no connection to this discovery.
• Option (b) — Maski edict discovered in 1925: Incorrect. Ten years after the actual discovery — another temporal-swap. The correct year is 1915.
• Option (c) — Maski edict discovered in 1915: Correct. This is the verified date of discovery. The inscription, found in Raichur district of present-day Karnataka, explicitly uses the name 'Ashoka' alongside 'Devanampiya Piyadassi,' settling the historiographical debate that had persisted since Prinsep's 1837 decipherment.
• Option (d) — Maski edict discovered in 1935: Incorrect. Twenty years after the actual discovery — too late.

Value Addition:
• The Maski discovery was made by C. Beadon, a British official, during an archaeological survey.
• Maski is located in Raichur district of Karnataka — in the Deccan, showing the geographic reach of Minor Rock Edicts into southern India.
• The Gurjara edict (Datia, Madhya Pradesh) is a second Minor Rock Edict explicitly naming 'Ashoka.'

solution.concept_anchor: Ashoka chose Prakrit over Sanskrit deliberate vernacular policy

statement_analysis.statement: Ashoka's choice of Prakrit for most of his inscriptions is understood as a deliberate communicative strategy to reach the common populace, given that Prakrit was the spoken vernacular of most of his subjects.
statement_analysis.reason: The scholarly consensus is that Ashoka chose Prakrit precisely because it was the spoken language of ordinary subjects, making Dhamma accessible to the widest possible audience — in contrast to Sanskrit, which was confined to the Brahmanical elite.

statement_analysis.statement: In the western and northwestern regions of the Mauryan Empire, Ashoka also issued Prakrit edicts but in different scripts (Kharosthi) and, at some sites, replaced Prakrit entirely with Aramaic or Greek.
statement_analysis.reason: The northwest used Kharosthi for Prakrit (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra), while frontier sites like Kandahar, Taxila, and Laghman used Aramaic or Greek — confirming that Prakrit was not universal even within the Ashokan corpus.

statement_analysis.statement: Prakrit as used in Ashokan inscriptions was a single, unified linguistic standard imposed by the imperial centre across all regions of the Mauryan Empire.
statement_analysis.reason: Ashokan Prakrit shows regional dialectal variation — Magadhi in the east, different features in western and northwestern inscriptions. Far from being a single imposed standard, it reflects the existing vernacular speech of different regions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is deceptive because statements 1 and 2 are clearly defensible, and students may extend the logic of a coherent imperial language policy to assume statement 3 (Prakrit as a 'unified standard') must also be true.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Prakrit as vernacular strategy — the deliberate communicative rationale is well-established; correct.
Statement 2: Kharosthi for Prakrit in northwest + Aramaic/Greek at frontier sites — accurately describes the language-script geography; correct.
Statement 3: 'Single, unified linguistic standard imposed by imperial centre' — this misrepresents the actual dialectal diversity; Ashokan Prakrit varies by region; incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, 3 incorrect — answer is (b) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 sounds like a natural description of an imperial language policy — empires often do impose standardised languages. The trap is that Ashoka used the regional vernacular in each area rather than imposing a single Prakrit standard. The dialectal variations in the inscriptions are precisely what make them useful for historical and linguistic geography. Students who see statements 1 and 2 as correct may assume an organised imperial language policy logically extends to standardisation (statement 3), but it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
Ashoka's Prakrit policy was inclusive but not uniform — it reflected regional vernaculars rather than imposing a single standard.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Prakrit was the spoken language of the Mauryan heartland and most subjects. By using it instead of Sanskrit, Ashoka made Dhamma accessible to the common populace — artisans, traders, farmers — who could not access elite Brahmanical Sanskrit literature.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The language-script geography of Ashokan Prakrit is complex: Brahmi in most of the subcontinent, Kharosthi in the Gandhara/Pakistan belt, and Aramaic or Greek replacing Prakrit entirely at select Afghan frontier sites. This shows deliberate adaptation to local linguistic realities.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Ashokan Prakrit shows significant regional dialectal variation — Magadhi Prakrit in the eastern inscriptions differs noticeably from the western and northwestern varieties. There was no single, centrally imposed Prakrit standard. These variations are, in fact, tools scholars use to date and geographically locate individual inscriptions.

Value Addition:
• The study of dialectal variation in Ashokan inscriptions is called 'Ashokan Prakritic dialectology.'
• Eastern Magadhi Prakrit is the dialect associated with early Buddhist canonical texts (Pali is closely related).
• Sanskrit's absence from Ashokan inscriptions persisted for centuries — the Rudradaman Sanskrit inscription at Junagadh (c. 150 CE) is the first major exception.

solution.concept_anchor: Inscriptions primary sources with official ideology limitations

statement_analysis.statement: Ashokan inscriptions are the earliest datable epigraphic records in India and thus serve as the foundational linguistic baseline for studying the evolution of Prakrit dialects in the 3rd century BCE.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard scholarly assessment — Ashokan inscriptions are the earliest large-scale datable inscriptions, providing the primary reference point for Prakrit dialectal history.

statement_analysis.statement: The disappearance of Greek and Aramaic from post-Mauryan royal inscriptions is consistent with the contraction of northwest Indian political integration following the Mauryan Empire's collapse.
statement_analysis.reason: After Mauryan collapse, the northwest fragmented into Indo-Greek, Shaka, and Parthian political zones — the centralized multilingual epigraphic programme ended, and Greek/Aramaic disappeared from royal inscriptions as Mauryan political integration dissolved.

statement_analysis.statement: Since Ashokan inscriptions represent official royal proclamations, they are equally reliable sources for understanding both the king's administrative ideology and the everyday religious beliefs of ordinary Mauryan subjects.
statement_analysis.reason: Inscriptions are primary sources for royal ideology but are inherently biased toward official positions. They cannot be treated as equal evidence for popular religious practice or social conditions of ordinary subjects, which leave few epigraphic traces.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'only Statement 3' is deceptive for students who correctly identify Statement 3 as problematic but then assume Statements 1 and 2 are also questionable, underestimating their accuracy.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Earliest datable inscriptions providing Prakrit linguistic baseline — well-established fact; correct (not to be chosen as incorrect).
Statement 2: Disappearance of Greek/Aramaic after Mauryan collapse reflecting northwest political fragmentation — accurate historical observation; correct.

Statement 3: Equating official royal proclamations with reliable evidence for ordinary subjects' everyday beliefs — this overclaims; inscriptions reflect royal ideology, not popular religion; incorrect.
Only Statement 3 is incorrect — answer is (d) 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the partial-truth technique: it correctly identifies inscriptions as 'official royal proclamations' (true) but then extends this to claim equal reliability for evidence about 'everyday religious beliefs of ordinary subjects' (false). Students who flag this statement may also doubt Statements 1 and 2 without cause, leading them to select options that include additional false statements. Precision in evaluating what primary sources can and cannot tell us is the key skill tested.
solution.final_explanation:
Primary source analysis requires understanding not only what a source says but what its inherent limitations prevent it from revealing.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ashokan inscriptions are universally recognised as the earliest datable inscriptions in India (3rd century BCE), making them the baseline for Prakrit dialectal studies. Their datable character (via Ashoka's reign dates) is what makes them foundational.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The post-Mauryan disappearance of Greek and Aramaic from royal inscriptions tracks directly with the political fragmentation of the northwest. Without Mauryan central authority binding these frontier zones into a single administrative system, the multilingual epigraphic programme ceased.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This is the false statement. Royal proclamations are authoritative sources for the ideology the ruler wished to project — Dhamma, piety, non-violence. They cannot be treated as equally reliable windows into the lived religious experience of potters, farmers, or merchants who left no inscriptions. The distinction between 'official ideology' and 'popular practice' is fundamental in source criticism.

Value Addition:
• The use of archaeological evidence (Buddhist stupas, terracotta figurines, votive inscriptions) alongside royal inscriptions helps historians reconstruct popular religious life.
• Post-Mauryan inscriptions from merchant donors (Sanchi, Bharhut) offer rare glimpses of non-royal voices in ancient India.
• Historical source criticism is an explicit dimension of UPSC Mains answers on ancient Indian history methodology.

solution.concept_anchor: Kharosthi script properties regional use and Aramaic derivation

statement_analysis.statement: Kharosthi script is written from right to left and derives its structural features from the Aramaic script of the Achaemenid period.
statement_analysis.reason: Kharosthi's right-to-left direction and its structural resemblance to Aramaic are well-documented; its Aramaic derivation is the standard scholarly position.

statement_analysis.statement: Kharosthi was used in Ashokan inscriptions to write the Prakrit language, and it is therefore a script, not an independent language.
statement_analysis.reason: Kharosthi encodes Prakrit — it is a script (writing system) for the Prakrit language, just as Brahmi is in most other regions. This script-language distinction is a critical exam-relevant point.

statement_analysis.statement: Kharosthi continued to be widely used across the Indian subcontinent through the Gupta period, eventually evolving into the Devanagari script tradition.
statement_analysis.reason: Kharosthi declined after the Mauryan period and has no descendants. Devanagari descends from Brahmi, not Kharosthi. Kharosthi's use was regionally confined and temporally limited.

statement_analysis.statement: Kharosthi's geographic use in Ashokan inscriptions was confined to the northwest — specifically sites in the ancient Gandhara region such as Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra.
statement_analysis.reason: Kharosthi-Prakrit inscriptions are exclusively from the northwestern Gandhara zone — Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are the canonical sites. Brahmi was used everywhere else.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all four' is deceptive because three statements are straightforwardly correct and students may miss the subtle falsity in statement 3 about Kharosthi's pan-Indian use and Devanagari ancestry.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 (right to left, Aramaic derivation): Established fact — correct.
Statement 2 (Kharosthi = script for Prakrit, not a language): Core conceptual distinction — correct.
Statement 3 (Kharosthi widespread through Gupta period, evolved into Devanagari): False on both counts — Kharosthi declined after Mauryan period; Devanagari descends from Brahmi; incorrect.
Statement 4 (Kharosthi confined to northwest Gandhara — Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra): Confirmed geographic restriction — correct.
Three correct (1, 2, 4), one incorrect (3) — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 contains a plausible-sounding conflation: students who know Brahmi evolved into Devanagari may accidentally assign this evolutionary chain to Kharosthi instead, especially since both scripts appear in Ashokan inscriptions. The second falsity (widespread use through Gupta period) compounds the error — Kharosthi was a dead-end script that disappeared from use well before the Gupta period.
solution.final_explanation:
Kharosthi is one of the most precisely testable scripts in the Ashokan corpus because its properties — direction, derivation, regional scope, and decline — are all distinct from Brahmi.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Kharosthi is written right to left, directly reflecting its derivation from Aramaic (also right to left). This structural link to Aramaic is the basis for its earlier decipherment compared to Brahmi.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Kharosthi is a script, not a language. It encodes Prakrit in the northwest — the same Prakrit language encoded by Brahmi everywhere else. Script ≠ language is the foundational distinction.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Kharosthi did not spread across the subcontinent and did not evolve into Devanagari. It declined after the Mauryan period — its last significant uses were at some Central Asian Buddhist sites (up to c. 4th century CE in those outlier contexts, but nowhere in peninsular India). Devanagari descends from Brahmi through Gupta and Nagari intermediate scripts.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Kharosthi-Prakrit is geographically confined to the ancient Gandhara region. Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are the two definitively identified Major Rock Edict sites using this script.

Three statements are correct — answer is (c) Only three.

Value Addition:
• Kharosthi was used for Buddhist manuscripts found at Bactrian and Central Asian sites (Gandhara manuscripts).
• The 'Gandhara manuscripts' written in Kharosthi are among the oldest surviving Buddhist textual documents.
• Brahmi's left-to-right direction contrasts directly with Kharosthi's right-to-left — a useful memory anchor.

solution.concept_anchor: Multilingualism reinforced centralised authority not political decentralisation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'accommodation of linguistic diversity' sounds like a sympathetic and historically plausible description of Ashoka's multilingual policy, obscuring the distinction between linguistic accommodation and political decentralisation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Multilingualism was not a marker of weak central authority — it was a deliberate tool of centralized messaging; describing it as 'administrative weakness' inverts its actual ideological purpose.

Eliminate (b): 'Accommodation of diverse linguistic communities through partial political decentralisation' adds an unsupported 'decentralisation' element — multilingualism was centralized messaging, not devolution of authority.
Eliminate (d): Multilingualism was not a temporary measure abandoned after consolidation — it was sustained throughout Ashoka's reign as a core epigraphic strategy.

Confirm (c): Multilingualism was 'communicative imperialism' — a single, centrally composed Dhamma message delivered in multiple languages to reinforce, not dilute, imperial authority across diverse populations.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) uses the term 'accommodation' which is factually correct (Ashoka did accommodate diverse linguistic communities) but appends 'partial political decentralisation' which is false. Students who read quickly or accept the first clause as accurate may not catch the false extension. The scope-extension trap adds a political inference ('decentralisation') to a linguistic fact ('accommodation'), making the option 75% true and 25% false — the classic partial-truth distractor design.
solution.final_explanation:
Ashoka's multilingual inscriptions are a deliberate imperial communication strategy — their purpose and ideological meaning must be precisely understood.

• Option (a) — Multilingualism as administrative weakness: Incorrect. The opposite is true: using multiple languages to project a single message across a vast, diverse empire demonstrates administrative reach and sophistication, not weakness.
• Option (b) — Linguistic accommodation with partial political decentralisation: Incorrect. The linguistic accommodation is real; the political decentralisation is a false addition. Ashoka's multilingual programme was centrally composed and issued — no regional interpretive autonomy was granted.
• Option (c) — Centralized message in multiple languages reinforcing imperial authority: Correct. Scholars describe this as 'communicative imperialism' — the same Dhamma ideology delivered in every language the empire's subjects could understand, thereby extending the reach of central authority rather than fragmenting it.
• Option (d) — Temporary multilingualism abandoned after political consolidation: Incorrect. Multilingualism is sustained across Ashoka's entire epigraphic career — from early Minor Rock Edicts to later Pillar Edicts (in their respective linguistic zones). There is no evidence of abandonment.

Value Addition:
• Later Gupta rulers used only Sanskrit — a single language for a single elite audience — representing the inverse of Ashoka's inclusive multilingual strategy.
• The contrast between Mauryan multilingualism and Gupta Sanskrit exclusivism mirrors a broader contrast in royal legitimation ideologies.
• The concept of 'communicative imperialism' was developed by scholars studying the intersection of language policy and imperial power in ancient empires.

statement_analysis.reason: The Kandahar inscription summarises Dhamma themes (piety, non-violence, obedience) but is NOT a direct translation of any single specific Major Rock Edict. It adapts and condenses Dhamma principles rather than translating them verbatim.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is deceptive because statements 2 and 3 are clearly true; students who know the Kandahar inscription is a 'translation' in general terms may not check whether it is a verbatim translation of a specific numbered Rock Edict — which it is not.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'Word-for-word translation of one of the fourteen Major Rock Edicts' — the Kandahar inscription summarises Dhamma themes, not a direct translation of any specific edict; incorrect.
Statement 2: Greek community engagement + inclusive communication policy — accurate description of the inscription's historical purpose; correct.
Statement 3: 'Eusebeia' for piety in the Greek text — documented in the actual inscription; correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct, 1 incorrect — answer is (b) 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is precise: students who know the Kandahar inscription relates to Ashoka's Dhamma edicts may loosely accept 'translation of a Rock Edict' without checking the specific claim of 'word-for-word' or 'of one of the fourteen Major Rock Edicts.' The Kandahar inscription is an independent composition that summarises Dhamma principles — not a translation of any specific numbered edict. The partial-truth technique makes the first part (it deals with Dhamma) true while the precise characterisation (word-for-word translation of a specific edict) is false.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kandahar bilingual inscription is unique in the Ashokan corpus and requires precise understanding of its content and character.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Kandahar inscription is not a verbatim translation of any specific numbered Major Rock Edict. It is an independent composition that summarises core Dhamma themes — non-violence, piety, obedience — adapting them for a Hellenistic audience. This is a crucial distinction that students often miss.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Kandahar (ancient Arachosia) had a significant Greek-speaking population, descendants of Alexander's soldiers and settlers. Ashoka's decision to issue a Greek-language proclamation here exemplifies his policy of tailoring communication to local linguistic demographics — a deliberate inclusive governance strategy.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Greek text employs 'eusebeia' (piety/devotion) — a term central to Greek civic and philosophical discourse — to render the concept of Dhamma virtue. This cross-cultural philosophical translation is one of the most studied examples of ancient East-West intellectual exchange.

Value Addition:
• Kandahar (ancient Arachosia) is in present-day southern Afghanistan — the easternmost limit of significant Greek demographic settlement after Alexander.
• The Seleucid Empire, Ashoka's northwestern neighbour, also issued multilingual royal proclamations — the epigraphic environment of the Hellenistic world likely influenced Ashoka's practice.
• The Kandahar inscription's content about 'obedience' and 'piety' aligns with mainstream Greek concepts of civic virtue, facilitating its acceptance by a Hellenistic audience.

solution.concept_anchor: Brahmi origin theories — indigenous vs Semitic derivation

statement_analysis.statement: The origin of the Brahmi script remains a subject of scholarly debate, with two main competing theories: one tracing it to an indigenous development possibly connected to the Indus script, and another deriving it from a Semitic (Phoenician or Aramaic) ancestor around the 6th–4th century BCE.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the indigenous-Indus derivation theory and the Semitic-derivation theory are real scholarly positions, and the debate remains unresolved. Neither theory has achieved definitive consensus.

statement_analysis.statement: The decipherment of Brahmi by James Prinsep in 1837 also resolved the question of Brahmi's origins, confirming that it derived from the Kharosthi script which was itself derived from Aramaic.
statement_analysis.reason: Prinsep's decipherment established the reading of Brahmi characters but did not resolve the question of Brahmi's origins — that debate continues. Moreover, Brahmi did not derive from Kharosthi; they are independent scripts with separate ancestral traditions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Prinsep's work was landmark and involved Kharosthi-Brahmi comparisons may assume his decipherment also settled the origin question, or that using Kharosthi to unlock Brahmi implies Kharosthi is Brahmi's ancestor.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Both origin theories (Indus-indigenous and Semitic-derivation) are real scholarly positions — Statement 1 correctly characterises the ongoing debate; correct.

Statement 2: Prinsep's 1837 decipherment did not resolve Brahmi's origins — and Brahmi emphatically did NOT derive from Kharosthi (they are separate scripts); the entity-swap (Kharosthi as Brahmi's ancestor) makes this statement false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The methodological connection between Kharosthi and Brahmi in Prinsep's decipherment work is frequently misunderstood as implying a genealogical relationship. Prinsep used Kharosthi as a comparative tool to decode Brahmi — not because Brahmi derived from Kharosthi, but because bilingual coins carried both scripts encoding the same sounds. The entity-swap trap replaces the correct 'Prinsep used Kharosthi as a key' with the false 'Brahmi derived from Kharosthi.'
solution.final_explanation:
The origin of Brahmi and the method of its decipherment are two distinct questions that must not be conflated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The debate about Brahmi's origins has not been resolved. The indigenous-Indus theory holds that Brahmi evolved from a lost writing tradition related to the Indus script. The Semitic-derivation theory argues that Brahmi was adapted from a Phoenician or North Semitic script around the 6th–4th century BCE. Both theories have scholarly proponents; neither has definitively won.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Prinsep's 1837 decipherment answered the question 'what sounds do Brahmi characters represent?' — not 'where did Brahmi come from?' The origin question remains open. More critically, the statement incorrectly claims Brahmi derived from Kharosthi — this is false. Brahmi and Kharosthi are separate scripts with independent ancestries. Prinsep used bilingual Kharosthi-Brahmi coins as a comparative key, but this methodological relationship has no bearing on Brahmi's genealogical origins.

Value Addition:
• The Indus script remains undeciphered — any claim of proven continuity between Indus and Brahmi must be treated with scholarly caution.
• Brahmi's earliest confirmed specimens are from the Ashokan period (3rd century BCE); pre-Ashokan Brahmi specimens are rare and disputed.
• The Semitic-derivation theory is more widely accepted in mainstream scholarship, but the indigenous theory has been championed by several Indian scholars.

solution.concept_anchor: Inscription type matched to language script and geographic zone
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly matches the two most famous pairings (Pillar Edicts/Brahmi and Kandahar/Greek-Aramaic) but swaps the third and fourth, exploiting weaker recall of the Kharosthi-Aramaic distinction.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Pillar Edicts: exclusively Brahmi-Prakrit in the Gangetic plains — any option pairing Pillar Edicts with Kharosthi or Greek is eliminated.
Anchor on Kandahar bilingual: Greek and Aramaic — confirmed unique.
Major Rock Edicts in the northwest at Shahbazgarhi/Mansehra: Kharosthi-Prakrit — not Aramaic.
Aramaic standalone (non-bilingual): Taxila and Laghman — these are distinct from Kharosthi-Prakrit sites.
Option (d) correctly assigns all four pairings.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The northwest has both Kharosthi-Prakrit sites (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) and Aramaic sites (Taxila, Laghman, plus the bilingual Kandahar). Students who learn 'northwest = non-Brahmi' without distinguishing between Kharosthi-Prakrit and Aramaic may swap these two categories, choosing option (b) or (c) which correctly match two pairs but err on the Kharosthi-Aramaic distinction. Geographic precision within the northwest is the key skill tested.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ashokan epigraphic corpus can be mapped onto four distinct language-script zones, each tied to a specific inscription type and geographic region.

• Pillar Edicts → Brahmi-Prakrit (Gangetic plains/Terai): Pillar Edicts are exclusively in Brahmi-Prakrit and are found only in the Gangetic-Terai belt (Delhi, Allahabad, Lauriya-Nandangarh, Sarnath, etc.). No Pillar Edict uses any other language or script.
• Kandahar bilingual → Greek and Aramaic: The sole Greek-Aramaic bilingual edict, located in southern Afghanistan. Unique in the entire Ashokan corpus.
• Northwest Major Rock Edicts (Shahbazgarhi/Mansehra) → Kharosthi-Prakrit: The Gandhara zone sites where Prakrit was encoded in Kharosthi rather than Brahmi. These are the only Kharosthi-Prakrit Major Rock Edict sites.
• Frontier standalone Aramaic (Taxila, Laghman) → Aramaic only (non-bilingual): Former Achaemenid administrative centres where Aramaic served as a standalone language — not paired with Greek.

The trap options swap Kharosthi-Prakrit with standalone Aramaic — the two non-Brahmi, non-Greek categories that students most frequently confuse.

Value Addition:
• The four-zone mapping (Brahmi-heartland, Kharosthi-northwest, Aramaic-frontier, Greek-Aramaic-Kandahar) is the master framework for Ashokan inscription geography.
• Pillar Edicts at Sarnath, Delhi (Firoz Shah Kotla), Lauriya-Nandangarh, Rampurwa, and Allahabad (Prayagraj) are all Brahmi-Prakrit.
• No Pillar Edict has ever been found in the northwest — a definitive geographic constraint.

solution.concept_anchor: Gupta Sanskrit shift — political religious ideology not linguistic evolution
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it invokes 'natural linguistic evolution' — a plausible-sounding process that students who understand language change over time may accept without applying the specific historical context of the Gupta ideological shift.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a dynasty whose rulers perform Vedic rituals, patronise Brahmin scholars, and present themselves as restorers of Brahmanical order — this is precisely the Gupta ideological profile.

Eliminate (b): 'Natural linguistic evolution of Prakrit into Sanskrit' is factually wrong — Prakrit did not evolve into Sanskrit; they coexisted as separate registers. The shift was not linguistic but ideological.

Eliminate (c): The shift to Sanskrit is not a 'simplified administrative language' — Sanskrit is more complex and elite than Prakrit. The rationale is prestige and Brahmanical legitimacy, not administrative simplification.

Eliminate (d): Sanskrit's adoption was not primarily for 'pan-subcontinent reach' — Prakrit actually had broader vernacular reach. Sanskrit was chosen for prestige and Brahmanical legitimacy among the elite.
Confirm (a): The Gupta shift to Sanskrit reflects a deliberate ideological choice — Brahmanical/Puranic legitimation of royal authority — not any natural linguistic process.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits a common misconception: that language change in inscriptions reflects organic linguistic evolution. The UPSC trap here is 'reversed-causation' — the actual cause of the Sanskrit shift is political and religious (Brahmanical revival), not linguistic. Students who understand that languages evolve over time may attribute the Gupta Sanskrit adoption to natural Prakrit evolution, which is doubly wrong: Prakrit did not evolve into Sanskrit, and even if it had, that would not explain a deliberate royal choice of script register.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gupta shift to Sanskrit in royal inscriptions is a landmark in Indian historical and cultural studies — its cause must be understood as ideological, not linguistic.

The scenario describes a dynasty that: performs Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya), patronises Brahmin scholars and Sanskrit literature, and presents royal authority in terms of Brahmanical Puranic legitimacy. This is the Gupta profile precisely.

• Option (a) — Deliberate ideological choice for Brahmanical/Puranic legitimation: Correct. The Guptas adopted Sanskrit to align themselves with the Brahmanical tradition of Vedic kingship, associate themselves with the prestige of Sanskrit literary culture, and signal a shift from the Buddhist/Dhamma universalism of the Mauryan period to Brahmanical Puranic legitimacy.
• Option (b) — Natural linguistic evolution of Prakrit: Incorrect. Prakrit and Sanskrit coexisted for centuries without either evolving into the other. The shift in inscriptions was not driven by language change but by a deliberate royal choice of prestige register.
• Option (c) — Administrative simplification: Incorrect. Sanskrit is more grammatically complex than Prakrit — it was not chosen for administrative simplicity. It was chosen for prestige and Brahmanical authority.
• Option (d) — Pan-subcontinent reach through Sanskrit: Incorrect. Prakrit had wider vernacular reach across the subcontinent than Sanskrit. Sanskrit's audience was the educated Brahmanical elite — a narrower, more prestigious group.

Value Addition:
• The Allahabad Pillar inscription (Samudragupta's prashasti by Harisena) is a defining early Gupta Sanskrit epigraphic document.
• The Gupta kings performed Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) — a Brahmanical ritual of universal kingship — and claimed titles like 'Parama-Bhagavata.'
• The contrast between Ashoka (Prakrit, Buddhist, universalist) and the Guptas (Sanskrit, Brahmanical, sectarian Vaishnavism) is a major theme in ancient Indian historiography.
